source.text: אַֽל־תִּ֭תְהַלֵּל בְּי֣וֹם מָחָ֑ר כִּ֤י לֹא־תֵ֝דַ֗ע מַה־יֵּ֥לֶד יֽוֹם׃

records.literal_gloss: Do not boast in a day of tomorrow, for you do not know what a day will bring forth.

en.L: Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day will bring forth.
en.B: Do not brag about tomorrow; you have no idea what a single day will bring.
en.R: Do not brag about what you will do tomorrow. You do not know what will happen.

decisions.choice: boasting about tomorrow: taken up in James 4:13–16
decisions.reason: James warns those who plan as if tomorrow were theirs. The verb "bring forth" pictures the day as giving birth to what no one can foresee.

source.text: יְהַלֶּלְךָ֣ זָ֣ר וְלֹא־פִ֑יךָ נָ֝כְרִ֗י וְאַל־שְׂפָתֶֽיךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: Let a stranger praise you, and not your mouth; a foreigner, and not your lips.

en.L: Let a stranger praise you, and not your own mouth; a foreigner, and not your own lips.
en.B: Let someone else praise you, not your own mouth; an outsider, not your own lips.
en.R: Do not praise yourself. Let other people praise you.

decisions.choice: stranger, foreigner: someone other than yourself
decisions.reason: The two words (zar, nokri) elsewhere mean outsiders; here they simply mean anyone but you.

source.text: כֹּֽבֶד־אֶ֭בֶן וְנֵ֣טֶל הַח֑וֹל וְכַ֥עַס אֱ֝וִ֗יל כָּבֵ֥ד מִשְּׁנֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: [The] weight of a stone and the burden of the sand, and [the] provocation of a fool [is] heavier than both of them.

en.L: A stone [is] heavy and sand [is] a burden, but [the] provocation of a fool [is] heavier than both.
en.B: Stone is heavy and sand is a load, but the aggravation a fool causes weighs more than both.
en.R: Rocks and sand are heavy. But putting up with a fool is even harder.

decisions.choice: provocation of a fool: the vexation a fool causes
decisions.reason: The word (kaas) is grief or vexation; it may be what the fool stirs up in others or the fool's own anger. This fool is the ewil, the stubborn fool.

source.text: אַכְזְרִיּ֣וּת חֵ֭מָה וְשֶׁ֣טֶף אָ֑ף וּמִ֥י יַ֝עֲמֹד לִפְנֵ֥י קִנְאָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: [The] cruelty of rage and [the] flood of anger, and who will stand before jealousy?

en.L: Wrath [is] cruel and anger [is] a flood, but who can stand before jealousy?
en.B: Rage is cruel and anger overwhelming, but who can hold out against jealousy?
en.R: Anger is cruel, and rage is like a flood. But jealousy is even more dangerous.

decisions.choice: jealousy: the fierce anger of one wronged
decisions.reason: The word (qinah) is the jealousy of a wronged husband in 6:34–35, which will accept no payment.

source.text: ט֭וֹבָהתּוֹכַ֣חַת מְגֻלָּ֑ה מֵֽאַהֲבָ֥ה מְסֻתָּֽרֶת׃

records.literal_gloss: Better [is] uncovered rebuke than hidden love.

en.L: Better [is] open rebuke than hidden love.
en.B: An open rebuke is better than love that stays hidden.
en.R: It is better to correct someone openly than to love them but never say anything.

decisions.choice: hidden love: love that never speaks up
decisions.reason: Love that keeps silent when a friend goes wrong does no good; honest correction is worth more. Verse 6 follows the thought.

source.text: נֶ֭אֱמָנִים פִּצְעֵ֣י אוֹהֵ֑ב וְ֝נַעְתָּר֗וֹת נְשִׁיק֥וֹת שׂוֹנֵֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: Reliable [are the] bruises of [one who] loves, and abundant [are the] kisses of [one who] hates.

en.L: Faithful [are the] wounds of a friend, but profuse [are the] kisses of an enemy.
en.B: A friend's wounds can be trusted, but an enemy's kisses come in plenty.
en.R: A friend may hurt you by telling you the truth, and you can trust that. An enemy may kiss you many times, but you cannot trust those kisses.

decisions.choice: profuse: many, lavish
decisions.reason: The word (naatarot) seems to mean "abundant": the enemy is lavish with kisses. Many take it as "deceitful", by context or from a similar word. The sense is close either way: the kisses cannot be trusted.

decisions.choice: faithful wounds: hurts that can be trusted
decisions.reason: A friend's hard words wound, but they come from loyalty (verse 5; 28:23). Compare Judas's kiss (Matthew 26:48–49).

decisions.choice: you cannot trust those kisses
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the contrast with the friend's trustworthy wounds.

source.text: נֶ֣פֶשׁ שְׂ֭בֵעָה תָּב֣וּס נֹ֑פֶת וְנֶ֥פֶשׁ רְ֝עֵבָ֗ה כָּל־מַ֥ר מָתֽוֹק׃

records.literal_gloss: An appetite satisfied tramples honey, and [to] an appetite hungry every bitter [thing is] sweet.

en.L: A full appetite tramples on honey, but to a hungry appetite every bitter [thing is] sweet.
en.B: One who is full turns up their nose even at honey, but to the hungry anything bitter tastes sweet.
en.R: If you are full, even honey does not taste good. If you are hungry, even bitter food tastes sweet.

decisions.choice: appetite: the nephesh as hunger
decisions.reason: As in 16:26; compare 25:16.

source.text: כְּ֭צִפּוֹר נוֹדֶ֣דֶת מִן־קִנָּ֑הּ כֵּֽן־אִ֝֗ישׁ נוֹדֵ֥ד מִמְּקוֹמֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Like a bird wandering from its nest, so [is] a person wandering from his place.

en.L: Like a bird that strays from its nest, so [is] a person who strays from {{gender:their|his}} home.
en.B: Like a bird that wanders from its nest is anyone who wanders from home.
en.R: A person far from home is like a bird far from its nest.

decisions.choice: wanders from his place: leaves home and its security
decisions.reason: The verb (nadad) is used of fugitives and refugees (Isaiah 16:2). The saying observes that a person away from home is exposed and without support.

source.text: שֶׁ֣מֶן וּ֭קְטֹרֶת יְשַׂמַּֽח־לֵ֑ב וּמֶ֥תֶק רֵ֝עֵ֗הוּ מֵֽעֲצַת־נָֽפֶשׁ׃

records.literal_gloss: Oil and perfume make a heart glad, and the sweetness of his friend [is] from counsel of [the] soul.

en.L: Oil and incense make [the] heart glad, and [the] sweetness of {{gender:one|a man}}'s friend [comes] from heartfelt counsel.
en.B: Scented oil and incense delight the heart; a friend's sincere counsel is just as sweet.
en.R: Perfume makes people happy. Good advice from a true friend is just as pleasant.

decisions.choice: the sweetness of a friend comes from heartfelt counsel
alternatives: a friend's sweetness is better than one's own counsel
but the soul is torn by misfortunes (the ancient Greek)
decisions.reason: The second line is hard. The small word "from" can also mean "more than", giving "a friend's sweetness is better than your own advice". The ancient Greek has a different line altogether. The reading followed here pairs a friend's counsel with oil and incense as things that gladden the heart.

source.text: רֵֽעֲךָ֨וְרֵ֪עַ אָבִ֡יךָ אַֽל־תַּעֲזֹ֗ב וּבֵ֥ית אָחִ֗יךָ אַל־תָּ֭בוֹא בְּי֣וֹם אֵידֶ֑ךָ ט֥וֹב שָׁכֵ֥ן קָ֝ר֗וֹב מֵאָ֥ח רָחֽוֹק׃

records.literal_gloss: Your friend and the friend of your father do not forsake, and the house of your brother do not go [to] on the day of your calamity. Better [is] a neighbor near than a brother far.

en.L: Do not forsake your friend and your father's friend, and do not go [to] your brother's house on [the] day of your disaster. Better [is] a neighbor near than a brother far away.
en.B: Never walk away from your own friend or from your father's friend; and when trouble comes, you need not run to your brother's house. Better a neighbor close by than a brother far away.
en.R: Do not turn away from your friends or your father's friends. When trouble comes, do not count on a relative who lives far away. A neighbor close by can help you more.

decisions.choice: and the friend of, as the scribes' reading has it
decisions.reason: The ketiv and qere spell this word differently; the meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: do not go to your brother's house: a brother far away
decisions.reason: The last line explains the middle one: a brother who lives far off is no help in a crisis; an old family friend or a neighbor close at hand is. The saying does not forbid asking family for help (17:17).

decisions.choice: a relative
decisions.reason: Readable uses "relative" to show that the point is family who live at a distance.

source.text: חֲכַ֣ם בְּ֭נִי וְשַׂמַּ֣ח לִבִּ֑י וְאָשִׁ֖יבָה חֹרְפִ֣י דָבָֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: Be wise, my son, and make my heart glad, so that I may return [to one who] taunts me a word.

en.L: Be wise, my son, and make my heart glad, so that I may answer [the one who] taunts me.
en.B: My son, become wise and make my heart glad, so that I have a reply for anyone who taunts me.
en.R: My son, be wise and make me happy. Then I will have an answer for anyone who puts me down.

decisions.choice: a son's wisdom answers his father's critics
decisions.reason: A son's conduct was his father's honor or shame (10:1; 17:21). A wise son is the father's reply to anyone who mocks him.

source.text: עָר֤וּם רָאָ֣ה רָעָ֣ה נִסְתָּ֑ר פְּ֝תָאיִ֗ם עָבְר֥וּ נֶעֱנָֽשׁוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: A sensible [person] sees evil; he hides himself; naive [people] pass on; they are punished.

en.L: [The] prudent sees trouble [and] hides; [the] simple go on [and] pay the penalty.
en.B: The sensible see trouble coming and take cover; the naive keep going and pay for it.
en.R: Wise people see danger and get out of the way. People who believe anything keep going and get hurt.

decisions.choice: almost the same as 22:3
decisions.reason: 22:3 has the same saying with small differences in the joining words.

source.text: קַח־בִּ֭גְדוֹ כִּי־עָ֣רַב זָ֑ר וּבְעַ֖ד נָכְרִיָּ֣ה חַבְלֵֽהוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Take his garment when he stands surety [for] a stranger, and for a foreign [woman] hold it in pledge.

en.L: Take {{gender:their|his}} garment when {{gender:they put|he puts}} up security [for] a stranger; hold it in pledge [when it is] for a foreign woman.
en.B: Take the garment of anyone who guarantees a stranger's debt; hold it as security if they do it for a foreign woman.
en.R: If someone promises to pay a stranger's debt, take their coat to make sure they pay you. Do the same if they promise to pay for a woman they do not know.

decisions.choice: repeats 20:16
decisions.reason: See 20:16, and on standing surety 6:1–5 and 11:15.

decisions.choice: taking a garment in pledge
decisions.reason: A cloak could be taken as security for a debt, though the law required a poor man's cloak to be returned by nightfall (Exodus 22:26–27). Anyone foolish enough to guarantee a stranger's debt should be treated as a poor risk.

source.text: מְבָ֘רֵ֤ךְ רֵעֵ֨הוּ׀בְּק֣וֹל גָּ֭דוֹל בַּבֹּ֣קֶר הַשְׁכֵּ֑ים קְ֝לָלָ֗ה תֵּחָ֥שֶׁב לֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: [One] blessing his neighbor with a loud voice in the morning, rising early, a curse it will be counted to him.

en.L: Whoever blesses {{gender:their|his}} neighbor with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it will be counted to {{gender:them|him}} [as] a curse.
en.B: Whoever blesses a neighbor with a loud voice at the crack of dawn will have it counted as a curse.
en.R: If you wake up your neighbor early in the morning by shouting a loud blessing, it will sound like a curse.

decisions.choice: a loud early blessing counted as a curse
decisions.reason: Praise that is too loud and too early is unwelcome, or shows itself insincere. Timing and manner matter in speech (25:11, 20).

source.text: דֶּ֣לֶף ט֭וֹרֵד בְּי֣וֹם סַגְרִ֑יר וְאֵ֥שֶׁת מִ֝דְיָנִ֗ים נִשְׁתָּוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: A continual dripping on a day of persistent rain and a wife of contentions are alike.

en.L: A constant dripping on a day of steady rain and a quarrelsome wife are alike.
en.B: A quarrelsome wife is like the endless drip of a leaking roof on a rainy day.
en.R: A wife who is always arguing is like a roof that leaks all day when it rains.

decisions.choice: contentions, as the scribes' reading has it
decisions.reason: The ketiv and qere spell this word differently; the meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: the dripping roof: as in 19:13

source.text: צֹפְנֶ֥יהָ צָֽפַן־ר֑וּחַ וְשֶׁ֖מֶן יְמִינ֣וֹ יִקְרָֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: [Those who] hide her hide [the] wind, and oil his right hand meets.

en.L: Whoever restrains her restrains [the] wind, and his right hand grasps oil.
en.B: Trying to restrain her is like trying to hold back the wind or grip oil in your hand.
en.R: Trying to stop her is like trying to catch the wind or hold oil in your hand.

decisions.choice: restraining her is like holding the wind or grasping oil
alternatives: whoever hides her hides the wind
his right hand proclaims oil (her quarreling cannot be kept quiet)
decisions.reason: The verse continues verse 15 and is obscure. The verb (tsaphan) means to hide or store up; here it is taken as holding her back. The last line may mean that oil slips through the hand, or that the scent of oil on the hand gives itself away. Either way, the husband cannot control or conceal her quarreling. The ancient Greek differs.

source.text: בַּרְזֶ֣ל בְּבַרְזֶ֣ל יָ֑חַד וְ֝אִ֗ישׁ יַ֣חַד פְּנֵֽי־רֵעֵֽהוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Iron by iron grows sharp, and a person sharpens [the] face of his neighbor.

en.L: Iron is sharpened by iron, and a person sharpens [the] face of {{gender:their|his}} friend.
en.B: As iron is sharpened against iron, so one person sharpens another.
en.R: When one piece of iron rubs against another, it gets sharper. In the same way, friends help each other become better people.

decisions.choice: sharpens the face: shapes the character and wits
decisions.reason: The face stands for the whole person as others meet it. Friends who talk, test and correct one another grow sharper, as blades do when struck together.

source.text: נֹצֵ֣ר תְּ֭אֵנָה יֹאכַ֣ל פִּרְיָ֑הּ וְשֹׁמֵ֖ר אֲדֹנָ֣יו יְכֻבָּֽד׃

records.literal_gloss: [One] keeping a fig tree will eat its fruit, and [one] protecting his master will be honored.

en.L: Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and whoever looks after {{gender:their|his}} master will be honored.
en.B: Those who care for a fig tree will enjoy its figs, and those who look after their master will receive honor.
en.R: If you take care of a fig tree, you will get to eat its figs. If you serve your master well, you will be honored.

decisions.choice: a fig tree: patient care that pays off
decisions.reason: Fig trees take years of care before they bear well. A faithful servant is rewarded in the same way.

source.text: כַּ֭מַּיִם הַפָּנִ֣ים לַפָּנִ֑ים כֵּ֤ן לֵֽב־הָ֝אָדָ֗ם לָאָדָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: As [in] water the face to face, so the heart of the person to the person.

en.L: As in water face [answers] to face, so the heart of a person [answers] to [the] person.
en.B: As water reflects a face, so the heart reflects the person.
en.R: When you look into water, you see your face. When you look into your heart, you see who you really are.

decisions.choice: the heart reflects the person
alternatives: a person sees themselves in others
decisions.reason: The saying is very compressed: "as water face to face, so the heart of the person to the person". It may mean that your heart shows who you are, as water shows your face, or that you come to know yourself by looking at others.

source.text: שְׁא֣וֹל וַ֭אֲבַדּוֹ לֹ֣א תִשְׂבַּ֑עְנָה וְעֵינֵ֥י הָ֝אָדָ֗ם לֹ֣א תִשְׂבַּֽעְנָה׃

records.literal_gloss: Sheol and Abaddon are not satisfied, and the eyes of the person are not satisfied.

en.L: Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and [the] eyes of humankind are never satisfied.
en.B: Sheol and Destruction are never full, and human eyes are never satisfied.
en.R: The grave always has room for more of the dead. People's eyes always want more too.

decisions.choice: and Abaddon, as the scribes' reading has it
decisions.reason: The ketiv and qere spell this name differently; the meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: Sheol and Abaddon: the realm of the dead, never full
decisions.reason: As in 15:11; compare 30:15–16. Human desire is as endless as death's appetite (Ecclesiastes 1:8).

source.text: מַצְרֵ֣ף לַ֭כֶּסֶף וְכ֣וּר לַזָּהָ֑ב וְ֝אִ֗ישׁ לְפִ֣י מַהֲלָלֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: A crucible [is] for silver and a furnace for gold, and a person according to the mouth of his praise.

en.L: [The] crucible [is] for silver and [the] furnace for gold, and a person [is tested] by {{gender:their|his}} praise.
en.B: The crucible tests silver and the furnace gold, and praise tests a person.
en.R: Fire tests silver and gold. Praise tests people: how they handle it shows what they are really like.

decisions.choice: a person is tested by praise
alternatives: a person is judged by what he praises
a person is known by his reputation
decisions.reason: The first line repeats 17:3. The second may mean that how people take praise shows their worth, or that what they praise reveals them.

source.text: אִ֥ם תִּכְתּֽוֹשׁ־אֶת־הָאֱוִ֨יל׀בַּֽמַּכְתֵּ֡שׁ בְּת֣וֹךְ הָ֭רִיפוֹת בַּֽעֱלִ֑י לֹא־תָס֥וּר מֵ֝עָלָ֗יו אִוַּלְתּֽוֹ׃פ

records.literal_gloss: If you pound the fool in the mortar among the grain with the pestle, his foolishness will not depart from him.

en.L: If you pound the fool in the mortar among the grain with the pestle, {{gender:their|his}} folly will not depart from {{gender:them|him}}.
en.B: Even if you grind fools in a mortar with a pestle along with the grain, you will not get their folly out of them.
en.R: You cannot get the foolishness out of fools, even if you pound them like grain in a bowl.

decisions.choice: mortar and pestle: grinding grain
decisions.reason: Grain was crushed in a stone bowl with a pounding stick to remove the husk. The stubborn fool (ewil) keeps his folly even under such treatment.

source.text: יָדֹ֣עַ תֵּ֭דַע פְּנֵ֣י צֹאנֶ֑ךָ שִׁ֥ית לִ֝בְּךָ֗ לַעֲדָרִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: Well know the face of your flock; set your heart to the herds.

en.L: Know well [the] condition of your flock; set your heart on [your] herds,
en.B: Know how your flocks are doing, and keep your mind on your herds,
en.R: Know how your sheep and goats are doing. Take good care of your animals.

decisions.choice: verses 23–27: one passage on the care of flocks
decisions.reason: These five verses form a single small poem. Verse 23 gives the command, verse 24 the reason, and verses 25–27 the reward: wealth and even a crown do not last, but flocks that are cared for renew themselves each year and provide food and clothing.

decisions.choice: the face of your flock: its condition
decisions.reason: To know the face is to know how things stand; to set the heart is to pay attention.

source.text: כִּ֤י לֹ֣א לְעוֹלָ֣ם חֹ֑סֶן וְאִם־נֵ֝֗זֶר לְד֣וֹר וָדֽוֹר׃

records.literal_gloss: For wealth [is] not forever, and if a crown [is] to generation and generation?

en.L: for wealth [is] not forever, and [does] a crown [last] to all generations?
en.B: for riches do not last forever, and a crown does not pass down through every generation.
en.R: Money does not last forever. Even a king's crown does not stay in a family forever.

decisions.choice: to generation and generation, as the scribes' reading has it
decisions.reason: The scribes' reading adds "and"; the meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: a crown: royal power, or wealth in general
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer no. Even the highest position does not last (compare 23:5).

source.text: גָּלָ֣ה חָ֭צִיר וְנִרְאָה־דֶ֑שֶׁא וְ֝נֶאֶסְפ֗וּ עִשְּׂב֥וֹת הָרִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: It disappears, grass, and it appears, fresh grass, and they are gathered, [the] vegetation of [the] mountains.

en.L: [When] the hay is removed and [the] new growth appears, and [the] vegetation of [the] hills is gathered,
en.B: When the hay is cut and the new growth shows, and the grass of the hills is brought in,
en.R: After you cut the hay, new grass grows. Then you gather the grass from the hills.

decisions.choice: hay and new growth: the farming year
decisions.reason: The hay is cut and stored for the animals, fresh grass springs up, and hill pasture is gathered as fodder. The year's cycle renews the shepherd's wealth.

source.text: כְּבָשִׂ֥ים לִלְבוּשֶׁ֑ךָ וּמְחִ֥יר שָׂ֝דֶ֗ה עַתּוּדִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: Lambs [are] for your clothing, and [the] price of a field [are] goats.

en.L: [the] lambs [will be] for your clothing, and goats [the] price of a field.
en.B: the lambs will give you clothing, and the goats will buy a field.
en.R: Your lambs will give you wool for clothes. You can sell your goats to buy a field.

decisions.choice: lambs for clothing, goats for a field
decisions.reason: Wool was spun for clothing; the sale of goats could buy land.

source.text: וְדֵ֤י׀חֲלֵ֬ב עִזִּ֗ים לְֽ֭לַחְמְךָ לְלֶ֣חֶם בֵּיתֶ֑ךָ וְ֝חַיִּ֗ים לְנַעֲרוֹתֶֽיךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And a sufficiency of the milk of goats [is] for your food, for the food of your household, and life for your maids.

en.L: And [there will be] enough goats' milk for your food, for [the] food of your household, and [the] life of your servant girls.
en.B: There will be goats' milk enough for your food and your household's food, and to keep your servant girls alive.
en.R: Your goats will give enough milk to feed you, your family and your servants.

decisions.choice: goats' milk: daily food for the household
decisions.reason: Goats' milk and the cheese and curds made from it were staple foods. The care of verse 23 provides for the whole household, servants included.
